body: Probably not as that would complicate the processing model for `<form>` quite significantly. In particular, the same origin policy exceptions `<form>` has today do not allow for these methods. Either we have to forbid them in cross-origin requests or require CORS somehow. Both of those restrictions would be a first for navigations and rather risky.

As a developer, I would love this feature. Those of us who are still interested in this sort of feature may want to make a new thread in the [WICG Discourse forum](https://discourse.wicg.io/) and post their use cases there.
Just know it's been attempted several times in the past and implementers have rejected it.
(It even used to be part of Web Forms 2.0.)

Indeed—if I recall, Hickson said long ago that there weren’t clear use cases for them…or was that for JSON form data? Well, either way, that’s why any chance of this happening would require assembling compelling use cases for them and marshaling both coordinated community support and a reasonable specification for the vendors. A tall order, but less likely things have happened…
I am pretty sure that the main reason implementers have rejected it is complexity.
@annevk thanks for the context, I suspected this would have came up previously. Where would discussion from the previous attempts have taken place? They would be interesting to read.
https://www.w3.org/Bugs/Public/show_bug.cgi?id=10671 seems to have a lot of it, though not as much the implementer angle.

As an update, https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/3577#issuecomment-374109222 still applies. We cannot bypass the same-origin policy and enforcing CORS is theoretically possible, but would require integration of that to some extent with navigation, which is completely new ground. Maybe if something like https://wicg.github.io/cors-rfc1918/ motivated adding such complexity to navigation this would become more feasible. But until that happens this isn't worth the significant cost unfortunately.

> In particular, the same origin policy exceptions `<form>` has today do not allow for these methods.

Thanks for your comments @annevk. Can you point me in the direction of where these exceptions are specified? Between GET and POST, they seem to have every property of PUT and DELETE covered; request body, idempotency, navigation, etc... does it raise a fresh security concern or is this a legacy issue where the specification that defines the exceptions repeats only the HTML 4 form methods by name?

> Either we have to forbid them in cross-origin requests or require CORS somehow. Both of those restrictions would be a first for navigations and rather risky.

To me, implementing PUT and DELETE with a same-origin policy seems like a sensible minimum viable product, which would at least allow web developers to create html clients for their own REST services. Implementer interest permitting, this could later be extended with CORS support for both PUT and DELETE methods (opt-out) and GET and POST methods (opt-in). Could you also please elaborate on why you previously considered a same-origin policy for PUT and DELETE forms to be 'risky', and whether you still believe this to be the case? How does this compare to, for example:

1. POSTing to a cross-origin HTTPS resource with an invalid TLS certificate configuration, or
2. GETting a resource when the network is disconnected/offline, or
3. POSTing from a HTTPS form to a HTTP resource?

HTML defines part of it and so does https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/. And yes, what HTML forms can do are basically the enshrined exception.

A same-origin mode would similarly be risky (and unclear) as navigation does not have that primitive. So you'd have to define what happens if you get a cross-origin redirect and how that would be handled and such. And come to think of it, there's also a couple POST-specific code paths that would have to be generalized somehow.

> HTML defines part of it and so does https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/. And yes, what HTML forms can do are basically the enshrined exception.

That is to say, the exception could be extended if the specification editors such as yourself thought it prudent? There is no immovable W3C charter issue, for example, or fresh security concern that does not apply to the existing methods?

> A same-origin mode would similarly be risky (and unclear) as navigation does not have that primitive. So you'd have to define what happens if you get a cross-origin redirect and how that would be handled and such. And come to think of it, there's also a couple POST-specific code paths that would have to be generalized somehow.

I'm afraid I still don't understand. Perhaps you could define what you mean by risky, or elaborate what some of the risks are? Is there an inherent problem or insurmountable issue with having to define how redirects are handled, or generalising code previously implemented to handle POST? Is this not still significantly less complex than CORS support?

No, the same-origin policy cannot be extended further as that would put servers at risk.

The risk is that there are a lot of corner cases to handle and navigation is one of the more broken concepts in the HTML Standard. Same-origin is probably less work than CORS, but it's still a lot of work.

To help with the discussion, there are two drafts. These are highly complete specifications made as a result of past reviews.

- [W3C HTML Form HTTP Extensions](https://www.w3.org/TR/form-http-extensions/)
- [Supporting PUT and DELETE with HTML FORMS](http://amundsen.com/examples/put-delete-forms/)

IMHO, the latter has considerably less complexity.
Neither of those is close to complete as neither goes into the detailed changes needed to HTML's navigate algorithm.

Hi everyone,

[Carson Gross](https://bigsky.software/cv/) and I have been working on a proposal to make this happen. It addresses many of the concerns that have come up on this issue, as well as blockers from [past](https://www.w3.org/Bugs/Public/show_bug.cgi?id=10671) [attempts](https://www.w3.org/html/wg/tracker/issues/195). 

The full writeup is here: "[Support PUT, PATCH, and DELETE in HTML Forms](https://alexanderpetros.com/triptych/form-http-methods)". I'd like to highlight two aspects of the proposal, in particular.
## Common Patterns

(1) A webapp wants to implement login/logout. Login is handled easily with a POST form, but proper logout support should be:
- Known to the client to be unsafe, so it doesn't cache or pre-fetch
- Known to the client to be idempotent, so it can be retried without user confirmation
- Not in violation of HTTP semantics (GET is for retrieval, POST is for sending data)

The ability to make a button that DELETEs a `/session` would satisfy these requirements, create the best user experience (no "are you sure?" on a retry), and give developers a more natural solution for logging out than the still-common logout link—the source of [a decade](https://x.com/Nick_Craver/status/296281730984316928) of [pre-fetching bugs](https://georgemauer.net/2024/08/01/a-heck-of-a-wild-bug-chase.html). 

(2) A social media webapp wants to implement "groups" functionality. Requirements:
- Groups have lots of sub-resources (i.e. `/group/123/members`), so all group-level operations need to be at `/group/123`, for clarity. 
- Admins can edit group details, but only the group owner can delete the group

The best way to model this is by using separate HTTP methods for editing and deleting i.e. `PUT /group/123` to edit the group, and `DELETE /group/123` to delete it. By doing so, the webapp can assign different permissions at the router-level, and re-use common permission functions (middleware, annotations, etc); if all unsafe requests have to tunnel through `POST /group/123`, they risk very common security mistakes like assigning the same permissions to updating and deleting.

Both of these examples are described in more detail in [Section 8](https://alexanderpetros.com/triptych/form-http-methods#Common-Patterns).
## Security and Navigation 

For same-origin requests, the browser should simply issue the request; for cross-origin requests, the browser should issue a CORS pre-flight request, and bail (loudly, with a warning screen) if the server does not affirm the request. 

Four years ago, @annevk wrote:

> The risk is that there are a lot of corner cases to handle and navigation is one of the more broken concepts in the HTML Standard.

and

>Maybe if something like https://wicg.github.io/cors-rfc1918/ motivated adding such complexity to navigation this would become more feasible. But until that happens this isn't worth the significant cost unfortunately.

In the time since, both of these have progressed. The [navigation standard](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsing-the-web.html#beginning-navigation) was updated, making it easier to modify, and [Private Network Access](https://wicg.github.io/private-network-access/) appears to be making progress, providing additional justification for implementers. We also consulted implementers about this proposal and were advised that adding CORS to navigation would be preferable to a single-origin mode (this does not imply their endorsement, it's just to note that we asked).

Adding CORS to navigation not only ensures that `<form action=/example method=PUT>` attribute inherits the exact same security benefits as `fetch('/example', { method: 'PUT' })`, while not opening up existing servers to new avenues of attack (since they're already available in JS), it also allows HTML authors to replace POST—which has significant CORS exceptions—with methods that are more resistant to CSRF. This would make the median web application more secure today, and potentially pave the way to replace POST with a more secure alternative in the future.

We outline browser behavior specifics, including the [CORS algorithm](https://alexanderpetros.com/triptych/form-http-methods#cors), in [Section 4](https://alexanderpetros.com/triptych/form-http-methods#Technical-Specification), and discuss security in more detail in [Section 5](https://alexanderpetros.com/triptych/form-http-methods#Security-Profile). 

We believe that this feature is essential to HTML, for a variety of reasons discussed within, and are interested in helping to move this long-standing request forward, however we can.

Deleted my previous comment because the suggestion was clearly half-baked. But I still reiterate my concern about introducing new form methods:  How will this impact users on browsers that haven't implemented it yet?

Current browsers only support GET and POST methods, and will **default to GET** when any other method is specified. So if your browser doesn't support `<form method="put">`, it will _behave_ like `<form method="get">` and submit its form data **on the query string**. This could lead to [information leakage](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/598.html) via browser history, server logs, referrer header, etc.

@mamund:
> adding here that it would be a good idea to consider how the ETag and Last-Modifed headers can be used to create conditional requests (e.g. avoiding the Lost Update problem).
> 
> see https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-validator-fields

It's an honor to see your comment on this proposal, Mike, I'm sure you know it's heavily in debt to your work.

In the RFC, validator fields are included in [response to safe requests](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-8.8-2), which PUT is not, consistent with the same RFC's stance that [PUT responses are not cacheable](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.3.4-13). I think that it certainly makes sense for PUT responses to be able to tell the client "this response is the resource and you can save it", the same way POST/PATCH [sort of can](https://alexanderpetros.com/triptych/form-http-methods#Caching), but at least as far as I can tell, that would require a change to HTTP as well as HTML. That's probably a bit more than this proposal can accomplish.

I am very optimistic that better method support will unblock optimizations like that one, because we'll have more developer data to analyze, a wider pool of people who would benefit, and less API work required to make it happen.

@jlunman: 
> Deleted my previous comment because the suggestion was clearly half-baked. But I still reiterate my concern about introducing new form methods: How will this impact users on browsers that haven't implemented it yet?

At a high level, I think it is more important to get the API right than it is to drive immediate adoption. If you believe, as I do, that HTML will be around for decades, then waiting a couple years before developers feel comfortable using PUT forms is fine price to pay in exchange for the decades in which forms will remain intuitive.

> Current browsers only support GET and POST methods, and will default to GET when any other method is specified. 

This is nevertheless an important concern, and one of the reasons why I recommend that people never do login with htmx, because it will cause information leakage on browsers with scripting disabled. I think it is _mostly_ resolved by a [polyfill](https://github.com/alexpetros/triptych), as the only people who would not be covered by this are users who a) use an out-of-date browser and b) have scripting disabled. Given the user profile of someone who browses the web with scripting disabled, I think that number approaches zero in very short order.

Another way to resolve this is just to add an `httpmethod` field, and also add support for the new methods to `method`, so that while this remains a live concern, HTML documents can do `<form method=POST httpmethod=PUT>` and then phase out use of `httpmethod` once old browsers are out of circulation. We'll see if the spec editors and security teams think that's necessary.

I was going to suggest a similar solution to @jlunman's concern by keeping the form owner's method as post and then putting the new method on the formmethod on a submit button. 

```
<form method="post">
    <input type="submit" formmethod="put" value="Submit a message">
</form>
```

This suggestion however backfired due to the fact that the formmethod attribute invalid value default is the GET state according to [Form submission attributes]( https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-control-infrastructure.html#form-submission-attributes ) within the spec:

> The method of an element is one of those states. If the element is a submit button and has a formmethod attribute, then the element's method is that attribute's state; otherwise, it is the form owner's method attribute's state.

If the spec were updated to allow for the invalid value default of a formmethod to then default to the form owner's method attribute state, then that could allow for what I was going to suggest to work and if the form owner method was invalid, then it could remain as the default of the GET state. 

Looking at your suggestion, since `formmethod` is an attribute for form submissions that may be specified on submit buttons, if we added allowing `formmethod` attribute to be added to the form element itself, that could allow for `<form method="POST" formmethod="PUT">` (I don't love it and it looks super hacky but it allows it) to work, because as of right now it would still default to the method of POST, which would avoid @jlunman's concern.

> At a high level, I think it is more important to get the API right than it is to drive immediate adoption. If you believe, as I do, that HTML will be around for decades.

This is very true, and I acknowledge that this feature request dates back well over a decade, and had the change been made back then, it would basically be a non-issue now. So I'd be pleased to see this finally move forward, even if it means I have to wait another decade or so before I consider it safe to use in production.

> I think it is mostly resolved by a [polyfill](https://github.com/alexpetros/triptych), as the only people who would not be covered by this are users who a) use an out-of-date browser and b) have scripting disabled.

There are _far more_ reasons why JS can fail than just being deliberately disabled by users. And it's one thing if it just means the site doesn't work right. It's quite another thing if it results in sensitive data getting exposed.

> Another way to resolve this is just to add an httpmethod field, and also add support for the new methods to method, so that while this remains a live concern, HTML documents can do <form method=POST httpmethod=PUT> and then phase out use of httpmethod once old browsers are out of circulation.

I like this. It fits with HTML's long tradition of being backward- and forward-compatible, so that neither users nor browser developers are forced to update in lockstep.

> There are far more reasons why JS can fail than just being deliberately disabled by users.

Great point. For instance it's hard (at least in my experience) to make sure that every single possible way that a form might enter the DOM is processed by the polyfill.

I'll think I'll add it to the alternatives section! I'll make note of possibly re-using `formmethod` at the top-level as well, @06b. I personally find that a bit more confusing than using a new name, but we could mention it. `overridemethod` could be a plausible name as well.

Per this discussion, I've [added a section](https://alexanderpetros.com/triptych/form-http-methods#override-method) about the possibility of including an additional `overridemethod` that overrides the `method` attribute. I think this is sort of an exciting possibility because it resolves my main problem with [the current polyfill](https://github.com/alexpetros/triptych)—that it can't emulate form navigation properly—and allows for a much smoother upgrade path using server middleware.

Hi @Delapouite! 

My long-term view is that HTML should support custom methods. This would unlock some very interesting and powerful [self-description patterns](https://alexanderpetros.com/triptych/form-http-methods#REST-in%20Theory) with relatively little burden on implementers. 

That having been said, this proposal focuses on PUT, PATCH, and DELETE support because:

1. The evidence of demand for these methods is abundant
2. These methods have existing specifications and implementations, so no HTTP work needs to be done
3. The API itself is straightfoward (extend the `method` attribute with three new values)

While I do talk about the possibility of custom methods in the proposal—they were even included in [a previous one](https://www.w3.org/TR/form-http-extensions/#introduction)—they have an API surface that needs to be studied a little more. For instance: how would the form decide whether to use URL parameters or body content? What happens if your custom method gets standardized with behavior your server doesn't expect? I think these questions are easy enough to resolve, but I don't want to to logroll them with support for existing, standardized methods, which don't have them.

I hope that the spec + implementation work required to make PUT, PATCH, and DELETE happen generates momentum for a robust custom methods approach, but even if it doesn't, those three methods alone still generate tremendous value for the ecosystem.

Glad to see this was picked up at the most recent meeting, I think this work would be extremely valuable, starting with PUT, PATCH, and DELETE which have the clearest mapping to the type of activity we'd like to express through HTML forms regularly, makes a lot of sense to me. 

I see there are some concerns about graceful degradation and I think it is reasonable to ask developers who want to use this proposed feature to be able to use feature detection (the implementation should present a way to support feature detection). Forms often have interactivity (and I'd anticipate forms which use PUT, PATCH and DELETE might be more likely to do so) so I don't think it is unreasonable to expect developers to handle detecting the feature and modifying forms accordingly. 

I agree that the demand for these types of methods is clear and abundant. There is a lot of "form-like" behavior that attempts to access either these verbs or emulate features that should be connected to these verbs without using the actual FORM functionality. We should push developers towards using FORM for form-like behavior and I think that this proposed change would significantly help with that.

I've made two changes based on feedback from WAHTNOT #10574:
* Clarified that non-redirect status codes should all be handled the same (i.e. 200 vs 201 vs 202). The server obviously still has to send the appropriate one, but the user agent should render whatever hypermedia the server returns along with it.
* Changed `overridemethod` to `custommethod`, in order to more deliberately pave the way for full custom method support.

@AramZS:

> I see there are some concerns about graceful degradation and I think it is reasonable to ask developers who want to use this proposed feature to be able to use feature detection (the implementation should present a way to support feature detection).

I would certainly support a JS-based feature detection mechanism, although I do believe that a lot of the feature's value lies in not having to use JS for it, hence the attempt to provide an [HTML-only feature detection mechanism](https://alexanderpetros.com/triptych/form-http-methods#custom-method) via `custommethod`. If you have any thoughts on what feature detection you'd like to see in the proposal, please let me know!

@hannah23280:

> So for the time being, what are the recommended ways to submit form with the PUT, PATCH and DELETE methods

I think the best way to do so is with a light hypermedia framework, like [htmx](https://htmx.org/) or [turbo](https://turbo.hotwired.dev/). While JavaScript is not capable of creating the experience I'm trying to push here—proper navigation—the frameworks I linked to have nice partial page replacement mechanisms that support all the HTTP methods, and it's a relatively small lift to go from those to this, if this proposal works out.

> Maybe if something like https://wicg.github.io/cors-rfc1918/ motivated adding such complexity to navigation this would become more feasible. But until that happens this isn't worth the significant cost unfortunately.

It's worth pointing out that Private-Network Access (formerly known as CORS-RFC1918) [is now on hold](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/pna-on-hold). See also [this more informal announcement](https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev/c/NCV3anf1KtU/m/WyL9rKjtAQAJ) by Google's @christhompson.
@alexpetros I don't think the change you're suggesting is going to be easy to implement/deploy, but I wish you the best of luck.

Hi, some thoughts.


PUT allows the client to set the current state of the resource.
> A successful PUT of a given representation would suggest that a subsequent GET on that same target resource will result in an equivalent representation being sent in a 200 (OK) response.
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.3.4

Multipart is an odd representation for this method, it is a container for many representations and often implies the content will be spread across many resources if multiple media types are embedded in the request. Note that the spec grants a lot of flexibility given to the origin to transform the request representation into other forms. That said, does it make sense to allow a single `<input type=file>` set the content type instead of using `multipart/form-data`? 

I'll note that `<form method=DELETE>` is an odd combination. @alexpetros why not create new HTML elements which are better constrained to the HTTP method's semantics? [You appear to make the argument](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/12330) in another issue that this is a hack for forms to be used in situations where the request will have no body but here it is OK?

Even though `custommethod` allows non-standard methods to be used in a request it does not prevent a custom method to later become a standardised method that causes behaviour change in how intermediaries handle it, affecting those websites. For example, I might use the custom method `FOO-BAR` which later becomes standardised to not have a response body and CDNs implement support for `FOO-BAR` where they don't forward through the body. Personally I don't like this feature as an existing work around exists for methods not being supported which is to use POST on another URI. Supporting it treats HTTP methods as a lookup key, or an extension of the request's URI, and not a component of HTTP with behaviour that can differ method to method through standardisation. For example, what would you expect `<form custommethod=TRACE>` or `<form custommethod=LOCK>` to do?

> Multipart is an odd representation for this method, it is a container for many representations and often implies the content will be spread across many resources if multiple media types are embedded in the request.

I disagree with your understanding here. The HTTP methods describe actions on a _resource_ (read: URL). One of the core principles of the web as that the server decides what constitutes a resource—multiple form inputs might, and usually do, comprise a single resource. Whether those form inputs are encoded as URLs, JSON bodies, or multipart form data is irrelevant. It's no weirder for this to apply to PUT (which replaces a resource) than for it to apply to POST (which creates or replaces one).

> I'll note that `<form method=DELETE>` is an odd combination. @alexpetros why not create new HTML elements which are better constrained to the HTTP method's semantics? https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/12330 in another issue that this is a hack for forms to be used in situations where the request will have no body but here it is OK?

Yes, it is a hack to use `<form>` when you want to issue an HTTP request to a single, static URL with no user input. [That should be a button or a link](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/12330). There are times when it makes sense to have form controls on your DELETE request, though, such as deleting multiple resources that match a certain criteria. For instance, this valid HTML form would allow the user to search all their emails that match a certain criteria.

```html
<form action="/emails" method="GET">
    <label>Earliest date <input type="date"></label>
    <label>Latest date <input type="date"></label>
    <label>Sender <input type="email"></label>
    <button>Search</button>
</form>
```

The same form, but with `method="DELETE"`, would allow them to delete all the emails that match that criteria. In both cases the form choices would manifest as URL parameters. I don't personally have a problem with DELETE bodies, they are technically allowed by the spec and I discuss them [in the "alternatives" section of the proposal](https://alexanderpetros.com/triptych/form-http-methods#Allow-for%20DELETE%20request%20bodies), but they are omitted from the main proposal in order to limit controversy and stick to the most expected semantics.

> Even though custommethod allows non-standard methods to be used in a request it does not prevent a custom method to later become a standardised method that causes behaviour change in how intermediaries handle it, affecting those websites.

This is a reasonable objection, which is why `custommethod` is [also in the "Alternatives" section](https://alexanderpetros.com/triptych/form-http-methods#custom-method). I do think there should be a way that developers can make use of the feature sooner than 5-10 years from now, when the hazard of an old browser defaulting to GET has sufficiently diminished. I am open to other mechanisms, but I don't think figuring that out needs to be bundled with this proposal. 

Custom methods are supported by HTTP and have been [considered for HTML before](https://www.w3.org/TR/form-http-extensions/#introduction), with non-standard methods explicitly noted as being for "private or experiemental use." To answer your hypothetical, `method="TRACE"` should simply not work. In general, the feature would effectively be for methods that have standardized semantics but no widespread support in HTML yet—a forwards compatibility feature. Another name like `futuremethod` could be appropriate as well.

> I disagree with your understanding here. The HTTP methods describe actions on a resource (read: URL). One of the core principles of the web as that the server decides what constitutes a resource—multiple form inputs might, and usually do, comprise a single resource. Whether those form inputs are encoded as URLs, JSON bodies, or multipart form data is irrelevant. It's no weirder for this to apply to PUT (which replaces a resource) than for it to apply to POST (which creates or replaces one). To give an example. If I have a resource that is configured to serve up images, why not have web browsers send an image with the file's media-type as the request's Content-Type header? I agree that the specification is flexible and `multipart/form-data` can be used, but it is unnecessary indirection in this case, thus my commend that it is odd (but not unallowed). Why I say it indicates multiple representations might be embedded in the request, is that the flexibility of `multipart/form-data` is it can send files with their media-types + HTML input data as text/plain, otherwise it is a simple key value format. You might have a todos resource that creates a todo when the user-agent POSTs a todo's details alongside some file attachments. `multipart/form-data` is a good media-type for that purpose. But wouldn't a server expose those attachments via a different resource to the todo's GET resource in practice? If I was to update one of the file attachments, why not use the new file attachment's content type against its own resource? So to be clear, my point is not that multipart cannot be used, or that there are not cases where it can be a suitable media-type, but that it is indirect for many purposes you might use PUT, which forces us to support the complexity of a less suitable media-type in our APIs. > Yes, it is a hack to use `
` when you want to issue an HTTP request to one, static URL. That should be a button or a link. There are times when it makes sense to have controls on your DELETE request, though, such as deleting multiple resources that match a certain criteria. For instance, this valid HTML form would allow the user to search all their emails that match a certain criteria. This is the first line from the HTTP spec on DELETE. > The DELETE method requests that the origin server remove the association between the target resource and its current functionality [https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.3.5-1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.3.5-1). The target resource is the resource referenced by the URI in question. You might delete other resources as a side effect of deleting the target resource, but you description implies you are using the target resource to filter and delete other resources. I think POST semantics are a better fit for the operation you describe. > The same form, but with `method="DELETE"`, would allow them to delete all the emails that match that criteria. In my applications, I've frequently adopted a pattern like:

`GET /things/{thingId}` -> returns a static representation of a thing, with links to related things, etc.

`GET /things/{thingId}/edit` -> returns a form wherein the thing can be edited.
`POST /things/{thingId}/edit` -> updates the thing with the submitted values, then redirects (303) back to `/things/{thingId}`.

`GET /things/{thingId}/delete` -> returns a confirmation prompt, or perhaps a message indicating why the thing can't be deleted.
`POST /things/{thingId}/delete` -> deletes the thing, and redirects (303) back to somewhere else (typically `/things`)

This pattern works great when we stop thinking of resources as _data_ and instead think of them as **commands** and **queries** that _act_ upon the data. For a user-facing hypertext application, reifying a "command" as a resource unto itself means you can use GET to retrieve a form that prompts for parameters to that command, and then POST those parameters for the command's execution.

Anyway, as I said, I don't oppose expanding HTML's capability here (safely). But Fielding's blog post (and the comments below it) is worth a read for some fresh perspective.

> Ok, and what if you need to also include metadata with the image like say a filename to use when downloading, information about the source of the image, maybe licensing information, etc.

This is IMO a valid case for PUT and multiparts/form-data. But since PUT is idempotent, trivial edits of the meta data would require the image to be sent in the payload as well. So in practice it might be more sensible for an API to break the meta data from the image upload into separate resources.

@jlunman What you are describing is embedding method semantics into the URL, a well-understood workaround for HTML's insufficient method support. It is not "inherently wrong," but its limitations are discussed in [Section 7.2](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/form-http-methods#ad-hoc-uri-semantics) of the proposal. The main problem is that it overloads the meaning of a sub-resource:

```
POST /things/{thingId}
POST /things/{thingId}/delete
POST /things/{thingId}/subResource
POST /things/{thingId}/subResource/delete
```

With the method URL hack, your server has to always disambiguate between a sub-resource and a command. That's confusing and error-prone to implement—you typically end up putting if-statements inside your router handler. With DELETE support, you can cleanly describe your server's API interface with just routes and methods:

```
POST /things/{thingId}
DELETE /things/{thingId}
POST /things/{thingId}/subResource
DELETE /things/{thingId}/subResource
```

Section 7 also demonstrates [the widespread demand](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/form-http-methods#rest-server-support) for proper method support, which as you note has useful safety and idempotency guarantees. Important to remember that browers _already_ support these methods, and servers use them all the time, they are just missing from the HTML form's `method` attribute. We would like to correct this to make these common web patterns dramatically easier for web authors to implement.

Yes, they can do that with unsafe idempotent requests, and no it is not dangerous. That’s the whole point of defining them to be idempotent – there is no difference between making the request once or several times.

A request for `DELETE /foo` and a hundred requests for `DELETE /foo` are semantically equivalent – the result is that the `/foo` resource is deleted no matter how many times you make the request. The same is *not* true for `POST /foo`, which is why browsers and proxies *can* automatically retry with `DELETE` but *cannot* automatically retry with `POST`. “RPC” does not mean “tunnelling”, it means “remote procedure call”. Hypermedia has nothing to do with HTTP method semantics. It has to do with the **server** telling the **client** which state transitions are available for the current resource, rather than the client making assumptions based on convention or prior knowledge. 
That's all. The method semantics are a _completely separate concern_ from hypermedia.

And I don't discourage "resources as data". It's true that if you're working with an API that treats resources as data, then HTTP CRUD conventions are much more relevant - _especially_ in the absence of hypermedia. And certainly, allowing forms to make PUT and DELETE requests would be useful in that context.

All I'm saying is that you don't **have** to think of resources as data. There's a different mental model that is equally valid, and aligns perfectly with the architecture of the web, and the original definition of REST.

In a traditional server-rendered HTML application, resources represent **application state** (that is, what "state" your application is in), not data.  And the available state transitions are expressed as hypermedia within the resource itself (links and forms). This is what the infamous unpronounceable acronym HATEOAS describes: Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State.  This treats the browser **not** as a runtime host for a client-side JS application that calls some APIs, but as a universal client application unto itself, whose UI is entirely driven by the server. This is the architecture described in Fielding's original REST dissertation.

There is a subtle disinction between deleting a **resource**, and posting a request to delete some underlying **data**. Neither is more correct. Just different.

Just as a thought experiment, consider the following scenario:

You have an HTTP backend that allows you to delete things via `DELETE /things/foo`.  And let's say this proposal goes through, and you can then write a form like this in HTML:
```
<form method="delete" action="/things/foo">
    <button>Delete Foo</button>
</form>
```

Great! No complaints.

But... suppose a new business requirement emerges: In order to delete a thing, the user **must** include a comment, explaining _why_ they are deleting the thing. How would you implement this requirement?

Maybe like this?
```
<form method="delete" action="/things/foo">
    <label for="reason">Reason for deletion:</label>
    <textarea id="reason" name="reason" required placeholder="Explain yourself here..."></textarea>
    <button>Delete Foo</button>
</form>
```

But where should the "reason" field go, in the `DELETE` request when you submit this form?

**In the Request Body?**
That feels like the most sensible place for it. But sadly this is not broadly reliable - particularly when you don't know/control all the intermediaries.

Per [RFC-9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-delete)
> content received in a DELETE request has no generally defined semantics, cannot alter the meaning or target of the request, and **might lead some implementations to reject the request and close the connection because of its potential as a request smuggling attack**. [...] A client SHOULD NOT generate content in a DELETE unless it is made directly to an origin server that has previously indicated [...] will be adequately supported. An origin server SHOULD NOT rely on private agreements to receive content, since participants in HTTP communication are often unaware of intermediaries along the request chain

**In the Request Headers?**
Maybe a custom request header like `x-reason: blah+blah+blah...`?
But request headers have effective size limits (which vary by client, server, and intermediaries). So if the user types a moderately long explanation, they could easily end up with a `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` error.

**In the Query String?**
Of course not. That would change the URL, implying you're deleting `/things/foo?reason=...` rather than deleting `/things/foo`.

The moment you need to convey anything remotely more complex than `DELETE /things/foo`, you have no choice but to embrace something like `POST /things/foo/delete`, which, according to some in this thread, would violate the holy purity of HTTP semantics! 🙂

Again. I have no beef with this proposal, nor with HTTP CRUD-style APIs in general.  What I'm pushing back against is the pedantic assertion that using `POST` for actions that _may_ have similar semantics to other HTTP methods is inherently wrong. It's not.
Pedantically, I feel like in that case you're `PUT`ting a tombstone, not actually deleting the resource.

> Pedantically, I feel like in that case you're PUTting a tombstone, not actually deleting the resource.

Let the bike shedding begin. 🤣

PUTting a "tombstone" is _even less_ semantically correct. That's like replacing a file with a new file that _says_ it's deleted, rather than _actually deleting it_. It makes it even harder for intermediaries - even bespoke ones - to reason about the request, as the actual operation (delete) is now hidden entirely in the request body, masquerading as an update, and indistinguishable from other PUT requests.

The "reason" field in my example is not a property of the deleted resource. It's a property of the operation itself. It may end up in an audit log or a notification email, or wherever. But it makes zero sense to `PUT` it to `/things/foo`. It is much more honest and logical to `POST /things/foo/delete` - meaning, you are posting a _"request to delete some data, for this reason"_.

Contorting your domain model to try to fit HTTP CRUD semantics is precisely the sort of thing that prompted Fielding's "[It is okay to use POST](https://roy.gbiv.com/untangled/2009/it-is-okay-to-use-post)" article in the first place.

The entire point of including the concept of idempotency in HTTP is to enable this behaviour. It’s a deliberate design decision that doesn’t need to be re-litigated here. See [RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics § 9.2.2: Idempotent Methods](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-idempotent-methods):

> A request method is considered "idempotent" if the intended effect on the server of multiple identical requests with that method is the same as the effect for a single such request. Of the request methods defined by this specification, [PUT](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#PUT), [DELETE](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#DELETE), and safe request methods are idempotent.

> Idempotent methods are distinguished because the request can be repeated automatically if a communication failure occurs before the client is able to read the server's response. For example, if a client sends a PUT request and the underlying connection is closed before any response is received, then the client can establish a new connection and retry the idempotent request. It knows that repeating the request will have the same intended effect, even if the original request succeeded, though the response might differ.

There’s no reason to include idempotency in HTTP except to enable this kind of behaviour. It’s a deliberate part of HTTP, put in there to explicitly allow automatically resubmitting unsafe requests. HTTP was designed specifically with this in mind.

@JimDabell That's fair. And I guess it really depends on the nature of the "failure". If the server responds with a 500 error, browsers do *not* automatically retry even a `GET` request.  But they _may_ retry a `GET` in the event of a network communication failure.  And per that same spec, they should only retry **once** ("A client SHOULD NOT automatically retry a failed automatic retry."), so that should alleviate any DDOS concerns raised by @matthewquinn.

Anyway, @alexpetros already stated this is not in scope for his proposal.
